claim: RKIP (PEBP1) expression negatively correlated with genes involved in cell motility (cell leading edge, cell migration, focal adhesion) and kinase-mediated signaling (regulation of GTPase activity, phosphotransferase activity) in breast cancer patient samples from TCGA.
source: Our analysis revealed that RKIP (PEBP1) expression negatively correlated with genes involved in cell motility (cell leading edge, cell migration, focal adhesion) and kinase-mediated signaling (regulation of GTPase activity, phosphotransferase activity) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TCGA patient data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: BACH1 is among the genes most inversely correlated with RKIP in breast cancer patient samples.
source: Among the genes most inversely correlated with RKIP was BACH1 (BTB and CNC homology 1), a pro-metastatic, basic leucine zipper transcription factor that is post-translationally inhibited by RKIP via let-7 (Figure 1A; Dangi-Garimella et al., 2009; Yun et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 1A and cited previous studies.

claim: Over 70 motility genes and BACH1 that inversely correlate with RKIP in patients are downregulated by RKIP in xenograft TNBC tumors.
source: Over 70 of the motility genes as well as BACH1 that inversely correlate with RKIP in patients were also downregulated by RKIP in xenograft tumors, suggesting these genes are transcriptionally regulated by RKIP in TNBC (Figure 1B,C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data from BM1 xenograft tumors comparing control and RKIP-expressing samples.

claim: BACH1 knockdown in BM1 xenograft tumors downregulates motility gene expression.
source: To confirm that BACH1 transcriptionally regulates metastatic motility-related genes in TNBC cells, we performed qRT-PCR using BM1 xenograft tumors expressing shRNAs against BACH1 in two independent mouse experiments (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from two independent in vivo experiments with BACH1 knockdown tumors.

claim: BACH1 directly binds to the promoter regions of motility genes in BM1 cells.
source: ChIP assays in BM1 cells to demonstrate direct BACH1 binding to motility gene promoters (Figure 1E, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP assay data showing BACH1 binding to motility gene promoters.

claim: RKIP significantly altered the functional capture of 30 kinases out of 248 captured kinases in BM1 tumors.
source: Of the 248 captured kinases that were present in both control and RKIP-expressing BM1 tumors from mouse xenografts, RKIP significantly altered the functional capture of 30 kinases (Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by MIB-MS analysis of control and RKIP-expressing BM1 tumors.

claim: RKIP inhibited 23 kinases and enhanced activity of 7 kinases in BM1 tumors.
source: Consistent with its role as a kinase suppressor, RKIP inhibited most of these kinases (23) including the previously identified RKIP target ERK2 (Yeung et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by MIB-MS data showing differential kinase activity and cited previous work on ERK2.

claim: The kinases targeted by RKIP were distributed across multiple branches of the kinome tree and not limited to a specific kinase class.
source: The kinases targeted by RKIP were distributed across multiple branches of the kinome tree and not limited to a specific kinase class (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by kinome tree visualization showing distribution of RKIP-targeted kinases.

claim: Functional analysis of the downregulated kinases showed enrichment for stress kinase signaling.
source: Functional analysis of the downregulated kinases using Metascape (Tripathi et al., 2015) showed enrichment for stress kinase signaling (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Metascape gene set enrichment analysis of downregulated kinases.

claim: Ingenuity pathway analysis indicated that most RKIP-targeted kinases are functionally related, with stress MAP kinases (JNK, p38) and ERK comprising the core of the network.
source: Ingenuity pathway analysis indicated that most of these kinases are functionally related, and the stress MAP kinases (JNK, p38) as well as ERK comprise the core of the network (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis of RKIP-targeted kinases.

claim: Community analysis identified three main protein-protein interaction subnetworks within the extended MAPK family: kinases upstream of p38 (TAOK2, MKK3, MKK6), kinases upstream of JNK (MLK1, MLK3, MKK4), and p70/p90 kinases downstream of MAPKs (MSK1, RSK2, and p70/85 S6K1).
source: Community analysis identified three main protein-protein interaction subnetworks within the extended MAPK family including kinases upstream of p38 (TAOK2, MKK3, MKK6), kinases upstream of JNK (MLK1, MLK3, MKK4); and p70/p90 kinases downstream of MAPKs (MSK1, RSK2, and p70/85 S6K1) (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by community analysis of protein-protein interaction networks.

claim: MIB data from BM1 xenografts revealed three members of the MAP3K family (TAOK2, MLK1, MLK3) that are reported to activate both p38 and JNK signaling.
source: MIB data from BM1 xenografts revealed three members of the MAP3K family reported to activate both p38 and JNK signaling: TAOK2, MLK1 and MLK3 (Chen et al., 1999; Dhillon et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2004; Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by MIB-MS data and cited literature on MAPKKK function.

claim: TAOKs primarily regulate p38 but may also activate JNK in TNBC cells.
source: Specifically, TAOKs primarily regulate p38 but may also activate JNK in TNBC cells, and MLK1,3 primarily activate JNK in TNBC cells but can also activate p38 (Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments with selective inhibitors or siRNAs against MAPKKKs.

claim: MLK1,3 primarily activate JNK in TNBC cells but can also activate p38.
source: Specifically, TAOKs primarily regulate p38 but may also activate JNK in TNBC cells, and MLK1,3 primarily activate JNK in TNBC cells but can also activate p38 (Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments with selective inhibitors or siRNAs against MAPKKKs.

claim: There is extensive crosstalk between different MAPK axes in BM1 cells.
source: Our analysis confirmed extensive crosstalk between different MAPK axes in BM1 cells (summarized in Figure 2F, also see Figure 2—source data 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments inhibiting p38, JNK, or MEK individually using small molecule inhibitors.

claim: The crosstalk between MAPKs involved both positive and negative feedback (e.g. the JNK-ERK axis and p38-ERK axis).
source: The crosstalk involved both positive and negative feedback (e.g. the JNK-ERK axis and p38-ERK axis) suggesting that the stress kinase network regulated by RKIP is a complex network, and targeting individual MAPKs may be insufficient to mimic RKIP pharmaceutically.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on MAPK crosstalk in BM1 cells.

claim: The degree of kinase activity does not correlate with metastatic potential.
source: Second, the kinases that are linked to metastasis ranged from high to low functional capture, indicating that the degree of kinase activity does not correlate with metastatic potential (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of MIB-MS data showing distribution of RKIP-targeted kinases across activity levels.

claim: The effective decrease in kinase capture for RKIP targets was generally less than 30%.
source: Finally, the effective decrease in kinase capture for RKIP targets was generally less than 30% (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of percent change in kinase activity from MIB-MS data.

claim: A four-drug combination (p38i, JNKi, MEKi, MLKi) at minimal dosages demonstrated a robust effect on invasion without a significant effect on proliferation.
source: Out of all the dual combinations tested, two combinations demonstrated a robust effect on invasion without a significant effect on proliferation: p38i + JNKi and MEKi +MLKi (Figure 3—source data 2, Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by high-throughput invasion assay data testing drug combinations.

claim: 4D-MAPKi consistently inhibited MAPK signaling (p38, JNK, ERK) across three different TNBC cell lines.
source: 4D-MAPKi consistently inhibited MAPK signaling (p38,JNK,ERK) across three different TNBC cell lines, while the effect of the p38i + JNKi and MEKi +MLKi dual combinations was cell line-dependent (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis of MAPK signaling in BM1, MB436, and LMB cells.

claim: 4D-MAPKi was not toxic to normal human mammary epithelial cell lines MCF10A and 184A1.
source: Notably, 4D-MAPKi was not toxic to normal human mammary epithelial cell lines MCF10A and 184A1 (Figure 3F, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by 2D proliferation assays in normal mammary epithelial cells.

claim: 4D-MAPKi at 1X dose significantly inhibited primary tumor growth in syngeneic LMB tumors in a dose-dependent manner without obvious toxicity.
source: At the 1X dose, the 4D-MAPKi combination significantly inhibited primary tumor growth in both syngeneic LMB tumors (Figure 4A) and xenograft BM1 tumors (Figure 4B) in a dose-dependent manner without obvious toxicity as all mice retained the same body weight (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo tumor growth measurements and mouse weight monitoring.

claim: Both undiluted (1X) and 50% diluted (0.5X) 4D-MAPKi suppressed metastatic lung colonization in syngeneic LMB tumors in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Both undiluted (1X) and 50% diluted (0.5X) 4D-MAPKi suppressed metastatic lung colonization in syngeneic LMB tumors in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by tail-vein injection metastasis assay data in LMB mouse model.

claim: Treatment of mice with 4D-MAPKi for only 2 days following tumor cell injection caused significant reduction in the overall metastatic burden ~5 weeks later.
source: Treatment of mice with 4D-MAPKi for only 2 days following tumor cell injection still caused significant reduction in the overall metastatic burden ~5 weeks later, suggesting that the inhibitor combination suppresses early steps of metastasis related to invasion and extravasation (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by short-term treatment experiment in LMB tail-vein injection model.

claim: The half dose (0.5X) of 4D-MAPKi potently inhibited bone metastasis in human BM1 tumors following cardiac injection.
source: Human BM1 tumors responded better to the 4D-MAPKi treatment than LMB tumors, as even the half dose (0.5X) potently inhibited bone metastasis, the major site of metastasis following cardiac injection of these cells (Yun et al., 2011; Kang et al., 2003; Figure 4F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by intracardiac injection metastasis assay data in BM1 xenograft model.

claim: The 4D-MAPKi combination improved survival of metastatic BM1-bearing mice following a 3-week treatment.
source: The 4D-MAPKi combination also improved survival of metastatic BM1-bearing mice following a 3-week treatment (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival analysis of BM1 xenograft mice treated with 4D-MAPKi.

claim: 4D-MAPKi blocked induction of a significant fraction of both Bach1 and motility genes in syngeneic LMB tumors.
source: 4D-MAPKi, like RKIP, blocked induction of a significant fraction of both Bach1 and motility genes in syngeneic LMB tumors (Figure 4I).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR analysis of gene expression in LMB tumors treated with 4D-MAPKi.

claim: Each of three human or mouse TNBC cell lines has a unique MAPK network topology.
source: Characterization of the cross-talk between different MAPKs in the RKIP-regulated network revealed that each of three human or mouse TNBC cell lines has a unique MAPK network topology (compare Figure 2F to Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental characterization of MAPK crosstalk in different cell lines.

claim: MAPK network topology can differ within the same cell line based on stimulus.
source: JNKi treatment did not significantly inhibit p38 in anisomycin-treated cells, whereas it actually activated p38 under serum conditions (Figure 2F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C ). These results suggest that MAPK network topology can differ between cell lines, or even within in the same cell line based on stimulus and highlight the importance of considering network topology in determining treatment efficacy.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments comparing JNKi effects under different stimulation conditions in BM1 cells.

claim: No single MAPK inhibitor even at maximum dose effectively reduced BACH1 expression across the three cell lines tested.
source: However, as our model predicted, no single MAPK inhibitor even at maximum dose effectively reduced BACH1 expression across the three cell lines (Figure 5H–J, left panels and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response studies with individual MAPK inhibitors in three TNBC cell lines.

claim: The low-dose 4D-MAPKi combination attenuated BACH1 gene expression in all human and mouse cell lines tested.
source: By contrast, the low-dose 4D-MAPKi combination attenuated BACH1 gene expression in all human and mouse cell lines tested (Figure 5H–J right panels, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A , Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR and western blot data showing BACH1 reduction across multiple cell lines.

claim: Both 4D-MAPKi and MEKi treatment significantly reduced metastatic burden in the lungs of mice with orthotopic LMB tumors, while p38i showed no effect.
source: Consistent with the in vitro data for the mouse LMB cell line (Figure 5G,J), both 4D-MAPKi and MEKi treatment significantly reduced metastatic burden in the lungs of mice with orthotopic LMB tumors, while p38i showed no effect (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo metastasis assay comparing different inhibitor treatments in LMB model.

claim: Following maximal inhibition of MEK in EGF-stimulated BM1 cells, the surplus flow from Raf approaches 30% of the initial input signal that can be funneled to a compensatory kinase network such as PI3K/AKT.
source: Following maximal inhibition of MEK in our model, the surplus flow from Raf approaches 30% of the initial input signal that can be funneled to a compensatory kinase network such as PI3K/AKT (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by network flow modeling of MEK inhibition effects.

claim: 4D-MAPKi only diverted ~10% of the incoming stress signal to a compensatory kinase network because MEK/ERK inhibition was restricted to less than 30%.
source: When we modeled 4D-MAPKi, on the other hand, it only diverted ~10% of the incoming stress signal to a compensatory kinase network (CKN) because we restricted MEK/ERK inhibition to less than 30%.
evidence: The claim is supported by network flow modeling of 4D-MAPKi effects.

claim: AKT activation has a threshold effect with minimal change in activity until ERK is inhibited by ~30% in EGF-stimulated BM1 cells.
source: The results show that, under controlled in vitro conditions, AKT activation has a threshold effect with minimal change in activity until ERK is inhibited by ~30% (Figure 6D, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response experiments assessing MEK inhibition and AKT activation.

claim: In EGF-stimulated cells, 4D-MAPKi inhibited ERK signaling by ~75% and AKT was maximally activated.
source: Consistent with this finding, when we tested 4D-MAPKi in EGF-stimulated cells, ERK signaling was robustly inhibited (~75%) and AKT was maximally activated (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis of ERK and AKT signaling in EGF-stimulated cells treated with 4D-MAPKi.

claim: In serum-stimulated cells, 4D-MAPKi inhibited ERK by only ~40% and AKT activity was actually reduced.
source: By contrast, in serum-stimulated cells, 4D-MAPKi inhibited ERK by only ~40% and AKT activity was actually reduced (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis of ERK and AKT signaling in serum-stimulated cells treated with 4D-MAPKi.

claim: There was no significant activation of p-AKT signaling in syngeneic LMB primary tumors treated with 4D-MAPKi.
source: We also checked the activation of p-AKT(Ser473) in the syngeneic LMB primary tumors treated with either the vehicle control or the 4D-MAPKi regimen. We observed no significant activation of p-AKT signaling in the primary tumors treated with 4D-MAPKi (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), indicating that the compensatory pathway activation is not triggered.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis of p-AKT in LMB tumors treated with 4D-MAPKi.

claim: Stratifying breast cancer patients by high RKIP (PEBP1) and low BACH1 expression or vice versa reveals a striking inverse association of RKIP with BACH1 and motility-related genes in ~60% of patients.
source: Remarkably, stratifying breast cancer patients by high RKIP (PEBP1) and low BACH1 expression or vice versa reveals a striking inverse association of RKIP with BACH1 and the motility-related genes in ~60% of patients (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TCGA breast cancer patient data.

claim: The motility-related target genes identified in this study were inversely correlated with RKIP in other solid TCGA cancer types including pancreatic, ovarian, lung, head and neck, and colorectal.
source: The same gene families were also inversely correlated with RKIP in other solid TCGA cancer types (Figure 7B,C) including pancreatic, ovarian, lung, head and neck, and colorectal.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TCGA data across multiple cancer types.

claim: Expression of other experimentally validated metastasis suppressors (BRMS1, ARGHDIA, NME1, and DRG1) negatively correlated with motility-related gene sets.
source: Finally, expression of other experimentally validated metastasis suppressors (BRMS1, ARGHDIA, NME1, and DRG1) (Zhao et al., 2015) also negatively correlated with motility-related gene sets (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by TCGA data analysis showing correlation between metastasis suppressors and motility genes.

claim: RKIP is deleted or lost in virtually all metastatic solid tumors.
source: One of these, Raf Kinase Inhibitory Protein (RKIP; PEBP1), is a regulator of Raf kinase activity that is deleted or lost in virtually all metastatic solid tumors (reviewed by Yesilkanal and Rosner, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a review article cited in the text.

claim: Reintroducing RKIP to metastatic TNBC cells blocks invasion of cells in vitro and inhibits intravasation and metastasis of tumor cells in vivo.
source: Reintroducing RKIP to metastatic TNBC cells blocks invasion of cells in vitro and inhibits intravasation and metastasis of tumor cells in vivo (Dangi-Garimella et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited study on RKIP function in TNBC.

claim: Loss of RKIP protein expression is associated with poor outcome in a variety of tumors including breast, prostate, and melanoma.
source: Numerous studies have shown that loss of RKIP protein expression is associated with poor outcome in a variety of tumors including breast, prostate, and melanoma (Lamiman et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited study on RKIP expression and clinical outcomes.

claim: Expression of RKIP in preclinical models enhances the response to chemotherapy as well as radiation.
source: Furthermore, expression of RKIP in preclinical models enhances the response to chemotherapy as well as radiation suggesting that RKIP can potentiate therapeutic efficacy (Bonavida et al., 2008; Chatterjee et al., 2004; Woods Ignatoski et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited preclinical studies on RKIP and therapy response.

claim: Targeting individual metastatic pathways at maximum tolerated doses using single or multiple anticancer agents can activate compensatory pathways that eventually overcome treatment.
source: Targeting individual metastatic pathways at maximum tolerated doses using single or multiple anticancer agents can activate compensatory pathways that eventually overcome treatment (Gallaher et al., 2018; Duncan et al., 2012; Wong et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited studies on treatment resistance mechanisms.

claim: High dose combination therapies that target single kinases across multiple networks can be toxic and are insufficient to enable long-term survival.
source: Even high dose combination therapies that target single kinases across multiple networks can be toxic and are insufficient to enable long-term survival (Westin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019; Robert et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited clinical studies on combination therapy outcomes.

claim: Approximately 100 metastasis suppressors have been identified, many of which also inhibit tumor growth.
source: To date, approximately 100 metastasis suppressors have been identified, many of which also inhibit tumor growth (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited review on metastasis suppressors.

claim: BM1 is a bone-tropic, Ras/B-Raf mutant TNBC cell line derived from MDA-MB-231.
source: To test direct regulation of these motility genes by RKIP, we performed RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) of transcripts in control versus RKIP-expressing xenograft tumors of BM1, a bone-tropic, Ras/B-Raf mutant TNBC cell line derived from MDA-MB-231 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B; Kang et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by description of the cell line and cited source.

claim: BACH1 is a pro-metastatic, basic leucine zipper transcription factor that is post-translationally inhibited by RKIP via let-7.
source: Among the genes most inversely correlated with RKIP was BACH1 (BTB and CNC homology 1), a pro-metastatic, basic leucine zipper transcription factor that is post-translationally inhibited by RKIP via let-7 (Figure 1A; Dangi-Garimella et al., 2009; Yun et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited studies on BACH1 and RKIP interaction.

claim: Metastatic progression is complicated by dynamic changes in tumors that undergo evolutionary change in response to cells and stresses within the microenvironment.
source: Metastatic progression is further complicated by dynamic changes in tumors that undergo evolutionary change in response to cells and stresses within the microenvironment.
evidence: The claim reflects established understanding of tumor evolution and microenvironment interactions.

claim: For solid tumors, metastatic dissemination of sub-populations of tumor cells throughout the body is primarily responsible for lethality.
source: For solid tumors, metastatic dissemination of sub-populations of tumor cells throughout the body is primarily responsible for lethality (Weigelt et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited study on metastasis and cancer lethality.

claim: Metastasis is characterized by many distinct biological processes such as tumor cell invasion, transport in vessels, and colonization at distant sites that involve significant cellular stress.
source: Metastasis is characterized by many distinct biological processes such as tumor cell invasion, transport in vessels, and colonization at distant sites that involve significant cellular stress.
evidence: The claim reflects established knowledge about the metastatic cascade.

claim: The commonality between signaling pathways in both normal and tumor cells has limited the efficacy of most therapeutic strategies.
source: The commonality between signaling pathways in both normal and tumor cells has also limited the efficacy of most therapeutic strategies.
evidence: The claim reflects established understanding of therapeutic challenges in cancer treatment.

claim: Triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) lacks effective targeted therapy.
source: Therefore, novel strategies for suppressing metastasis are needed, particularly for cancers such as triple negative breast cancer (ER-, PR-, HER2low; TNBC) that lack effective targeted therapy.
evidence: The claim reflects established clinical knowledge about TNBC treatment options.

claim: Biological metastasis suppressors are proteins that inhibit various steps of metastasis and are lost or silenced in metastatic tumors.
source: Biological metastasis suppressors are proteins that inhibit various steps of metastasis and are lost or silenced in metastatic tumors (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited review on metastasis suppressors.

claim: RKIP functions like a low-dose, non-toxic drug combination that reduces the activity of several key kinases within a driver network to inhibit metastasis.
source: These results indicate that, in contrast to the common therapeutic practice of fully inhibiting individual kinases at the maximum-tolerated dose, RKIP functions like a low-dose, non-toxic drug combination that reduces the activity of several key kinases within a driver network to inhibit metastasis (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental data on RKIP's mechanism of action.

claim: The three MAPKs (JNK, p38, and ERK) as well as their upstream regulators and downstream effectors comprise the core RKIP-regulated network that drives metastasis in TNBCs.
source: These results indicate that the three MAPKs (JNK, p38, and ERK) as well as their upstream regulators and downstream effectors comprise the core RKIP-regulated network that drives metastasis in TNBCs.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from MIB-MS and pathway analysis data.

claim: MLKs and TAOKs as well as p38 and JNK have been previously shown to regulate cell motility and invasion.
source: MLKs and TAOKs as well as p38 and JNK have been previously shown to regulate cell motility and invasion (Cronan et al., 2012; Iizuka et al., 2021; Koul et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited studies on kinase functions in cell motility.

claim: Reducing BACH1 expression in TNBC increased oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria, mirroring the RKIP phenotype.
source: Our previous work similarly showed that reducing BACH1 expression in TNBC increased oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria, mirroring the RKIP phenotype (Lee et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited previous study by the authors.

claim: BACH1 gene expression positively correlates with RKIP-inhibited motility genes in both patient samples and xenograft TNBC tumors.
source: Indeed, BACH1 gene expression positively correlates with RKIP-inhibited motility genes in both patient samples and xenograft TNBC tumors (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of TCGA and RNA-seq data.

claim: ENCODE and ChIP-seq analysis shows BACH1 binding to the promoter regions of several motility genes.
source: ENCODE and ChIP-seq analysis in BM1 cells shows BACH1 binding to the promoter regions of several motility genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C; Landt et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by ENCODE database analysis and ChIP-seq experiments.

claim: The RNA-seq analysis revealed upregulation of genes related to mitochondrial metabolism and oxidative phosphorylation in RKIP-expressing BM1 tumors.
source: The RNA-seq analysis also revealed upregulation of genes related to mitochondrial metabolism and oxidative phosphorylation in RKIP-expressing BM1 tumors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and gene set enrichment analysis.

claim: The mitochondrial gene targets of RKIP positively correlated with RKIP, while negatively correlating with BACH1 gene expression in breast cancer patients.
source: Moreover, the mitochondrial gene targets of RKIP positively correlated with RKIP, while negatively correlating with BACH1 gene expression in breast cancer patients (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of TCGA patient data.

claim: RKIP inhibits the upstream TAOKs and MLKs in addition to Raf in TNBC tumors, thereby preventing activation of the pro-invasive stress MAPKs p38 and JNK in TNBC cells.
source: These data suggest that RKIP inhibits the upstream TAOKs and MLKs in addition to Raf in TNBC tumors, thereby preventing activation of the pro-invasive stress MAPKs p38 and JNK in TNBC cells.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of MIB-MS and inhibitor/siRNA experimental data.

claim: The stress kinase network regulated by RKIP is a complex network, and targeting individual MAPKs may be insufficient to mimic RKIP pharmaceutically.
source: The crosstalk involved both positive and negative feedback (e.g. the JNK-ERK axis and p38-ERK axis) suggesting that the stress kinase network regulated by RKIP is a complex network, and targeting individual MAPKs may be insufficient to mimic RKIP pharmaceutically.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from experimental data on MAPK crosstalk.

claim: RKIP suppresses the signaling capacity of multiple kinases within a key driver network, the stress MAPK network.
source: First, as noted above, RKIP suppresses the signaling capacity of multiple kinases within a key driver network, the stress MAPK network.
evidence: The claim summarizes findings from MIB-MS and functional studies.

claim: The 4D-MAPKi combination is an effective, well-tolerated anti-invasive therapy that mimics the strategy by which RKIP inhibits the MAPK network.
source: These findings suggest that the 4D-MAPKi combination is an effective, well-tolerated anti-invasive therapy that mimics the strategy by which RKIP inhibits the MAPK network.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from in vitro invasion and proliferation assays.

claim: The low-dose drug combination, 4D-MAPKi, suppresses TNBC metastasis by reducing the signaling capacity of the stress MAPK network that transcriptionally activates metastatic genes, thereby increasing survival.
source: These findings indicate that the low-dose drug combination, 4D-MAPKi, suppresses TNBC metastasis by reducing the signaling capacity of the stress MAPK network that transcriptionally activates metastatic genes, thereby increasing survival.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from in vivo metastasis and survival studies.

claim: 4D-MAPKi more effectively regulates BACH1 expression across cells with different MAPK network topologies than single high-dose inhibitors.
source: These data indicate that 4D-MAPKi more effectively regulates BACH1 expression across cells with different MAPK network topologies than single high-dose inhibitors.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from experiments testing BACH1 expression in multiple cell lines.

claim: Multidrug combinations are more effective at suppressing signaling across cells with different MAPK network topologies according to mathematical modeling.
source: The model suggests that multidrug combinations are more effective at suppressing signaling across cells with different MAPK network topologies.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion from network flow modeling analysis.

claim: Minimizing the inhibition of each kinase enables dissipation of excess signal so that compensatory networks are not activated.
source: In addition, minimizing the inhibition of each kinase enables dissipation of excess signal so that compensatory networks are not activated.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion from network flow modeling and experimental validation.

claim: Recurrence through activation of p-AKT after treatment of cells with MEK inhibitor is a threshold effect.
source: Indeed, our experimental findings support these general principles, demonstrating that different TNBC cells have different MAPK network topologies and respond in diverse ways to MAPK inhibitors. Our data demonstrate that recurrence through activation of p-AKT after treatment of cells with MEK inhibitor is a threshold effect, and p-AKT is not induced by the four-drug combination in mice, further supporting the relevance of our proposal and opening a new avenue of investigation aimed at finding the range of topologies within a single driver network and their relationship to multiple compensatory driver networks.
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response experiments showing threshold activation of AKT.

claim: p-AKT is not induced by the four-drug combination in mice.
source: Our data demonstrate that recurrence through activation of p-AKT after treatment of cells with MEK inhibitor is a threshold effect, and p-AKT is not induced by the four-drug combination in mice, further supporting the relevance of our proposal and opening a new avenue of investigation aimed at finding the range of topologies within a single driver network and their relationship to multiple compensatory driver networks.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis of p-AKT in treated tumors.

claim: A limited 2-day treatment with 4D-MAPKi after tail vein injection suppressed metastatic growth, suggesting that 4D-MAPKi primarily affects the early steps of metastatic seeding such as extravasation, invasion, or colonization.
source: Even a limited 2-day treatment with drug after tail vein injection suppressed metastatic growth, suggesting that 4D-MAPKi primarily affects the early steps of metastatic seeding such as extravasation, invasion, or colonization.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of short-term treatment experiment results.

claim: The RKIP/BACH1/motility gene axis identifies breast cancer patients who would be therapeutic candidates for 4D-MAPKi treatment.
source: These data suggest that the RKIP/BACH1/motility gene axis identifies breast cancer patients who would be therapeutic candidates for 4D-MAPKi treatment.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from TCGA patient data analysis showing inverse correlation patterns.

claim: BACH1-regulated motility-related machinery is a hallmark of metastasis that is targeted by multiple physiological suppressors such as RKIP.
source: These clinical analyses suggest that BACH1-regulated motility-related machinery is a hallmark of metastasis that is targeted by multiple physiological suppressors such as RKIP.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from TCGA analysis showing correlation of multiple metastasis suppressors with motility genes.

claim: Stress as an input activates the core MAPK network, leading to induction of BACH1 expression as an output which in turn activates motility-related genes required for invasion and metastasis.
source: Taken together, our results show that stress as an input activates the core MAPK network, leading to induction of BACH1 expression as an output which in turn activates motility-related genes required for invasion and metastasis (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is a summary of the overall findings from the study.

claim: Inhibition of the MAPK network by metastasis suppressors such as RKIP or a low-dose four-drug combination effectively restricts expression of invasive genes and reduces the metastatic phenotype.
source: Inhibition of this network by metastasis suppressors such as RKIP or a low-dose four-drug combination effectively restricts expression of invasive genes and reduces the metastatic phenotype.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion from the study's findings.
